item.title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
item.description: arXiv:2610.37927v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Vishal Upendran, Banafsheh Ferdousi

item.title: The Pointing Error Due To Laser Propagation in Space Plasma for TianQin Gravitational Wave Detection
item.description: arXiv:2610.39587v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: TianQin, a space-borne gravitational wave observatory, is designed to detect gravitational-wave signals via laser interferometry. As the inhomogeneous space plasma surrounds the inter-satellite laser links, the propagation of the laser in space plasma can introduce pointing error noise. In this work, we quantitatively assess the effect of plasma on the pointing accuracy of TQ's inter-satellite laser links. We employ a magnetohydrodynamic model to simulate the plasma distribution around the TQ orbit for different orbital orientations. Using the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method to conduct the ray-tracing calculations over a TQ orbital cycle under a solar wind dynamic pressure close to the 23-year average, we find that the plasma-induced laser deflection angle and pointing eccentricity are on the order of $10^{-20} \ \mathrm{rad}$ and picometers, respectively. These values are significantly lower than TQ's requirements. Our results demonstrate that the impact of space plasma on TQ's pointing error is negligible in moderate space weather conditions, indicating a positive outlook for the TQ mission.
item.dc:creator: S. W. Zhou, W. Su, S. Y. Zhou, C. F. Li, J. X Zhang

item.title: Excursion-set structure factor of the auroral electric field
item.description: arXiv:2606.26854v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A spacecraft crossing the aurora cannot tell whether structures in the field-aligned currents are short-lived or merely small. However, by tracking clusters of coherent radar echoes from aurorae and Fourier-transforming motion-shifted echo pairs across radar snapshots, we can calculate the dynamic structure factor of the point-clouds, thereby quantifying the auroral electric field's spatial power and its persistence from 5 to 40 km, in regions where the radar look-direction is perpendicular to the geomagnetic field. This follows from the fact that coherent E-region radar echoes appear only where the ionospheric electric field exceeds the Farley-Buneman instability threshold, and so a point-target imaging radar naturally samples the field's excursion set; the field's spatiotemporal correlations are discernible from that point process. We find that the echo pattern moves with its cluster: large-scale structures persist for tens of seconds, but scales under 10 km renew within seconds, and conjunctions with Swarm satellite pairs replicate the same scale dependence in field-aligned currents. Coherent radar can thus quantify multi-scale variability in the auroral electric field on Alfv\'enic timescales.
item.dc:creator: Magnus F Ivarsen, Kaili Song, Jean-Pierre St-Maurice, Glenn C Hussey

item.title: Cascade models of anisotropic turbulence in magnetized plasma of solar wind
item.description: arXiv:2609.10418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The solar wind plasma is modeled as a collection of discrete domains, each possessing local rotational symmetry about its domain-mean magnetic field. Based on this partial symmetry, we construct cascade models governed by the nonlinear and Alfv\'enic time scales. We introduce a stochastic renewal process with a bimodal waiting-time distribution determined by these two time scales. This process yields a two-branch renormalization solution for the total energy: a statistically robust branch with an Iroshnikov-Kraichnan-like $k^{-3/2}$ spectrum and a statistically marginal branch with a Kolmogorov-like $k^{-5/3}$ spectrum. Whenever energy-flux fluctuations become supercritical, the system selects the faster of the two available cascade rates, thereby preventing flux accumulation. During solar wind expansion, the system undergoes a dynamical first-order phase transition from the slow $k^{-3/2}$ cascade to the fast $k^{-5/3}$ cascade, with switchbacks accelerating the transition. The mixing of subcritical and supercritical domains in raw spacecraft measurements produces an apparent decoupling of the velocity and magnetic-field spectral indices. Incorporating a magnetic helicity cascade slaved to the energy cascade, we show that the large-scale spectra decouple into $k^{-3/4}$ magnetic and $k^{-3/2}$ kinetic spectra. For switchbacks inside the upper solar corona, the corresponding large-scale spectra instead decouple into $k^{-2/3}$ magnetic and $k^{-5/3}$ kinetic spectra. Data from Voyager, Ulysses, Helios, Wind, and PSP confirm the spectral signatures across heliospheric regions spanning heliocentric distances from 0.056 to 140 AU.
item.dc:creator: A. Bershadskii

item.title: Spectral properties of mesoscale fluctuations in interplanetary coronal mass ejections
item.description: arXiv:2607.23742v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Magnetic fields in interplanetary coronal mass ejections (ICMEs) often display a flux rope structure at large scales and a turbulent cascade of fluctuations at smaller scales. However, the nature of fluctuations at transition scales between the flux rope and turbulence - i.e., at mesoscales - has not been previously examined in detail. Mesoscale fluctuations of the magnetic field in 142 ICME intervals with clear flux rope signatures at 1 au have been examined using wavelet power spectra, with "mesoscale" defined here as spacecraft-frame frequencies $10^{-4}\ \text{Hz}<f_\mathrm{sc}< 10^{-3}\ \text{Hz}$, equivalent to timescales $2.8\ \text{hr}\gtrsim \tau \gtrsim 17\ \text{min}$. The spectra were found to be significantly less steep at mesoscales than at larger and smaller scales, with an average spectral slope close to $-1$ at these intermediate scales. The mesoscale fluctuations had relatively high cross helicity magnitudes and low compressibility, suggesting a significant degree of Alfv\'enicity, while also having more negative residual energy than the turbulent fluctuations found at smaller scales. Uncertainties in the spectral slope values at mesoscales were used to distinguish between spectra showing a relatively smooth power-law behavior or (less commonly) a more bumpy trend; the smoother power-law intervals had a balanced cross helicity distribution while the more bumpy spectra had a predominantly antisunward cross helicity. Slow wind intervals were similarly analyzed, and showed similar properties to the ICMEs. These results indicate that a spectrally narrow $1/f$ range is typically present in ICMEs at mesoscales.
item.dc:creator: Anna-Sofia Jylh\"a, Simon Good, Emilia Kilpua
